examples: Anyone can apply, regardless of experience.
The match will be held regardless of rain.
Please let us know whether or not you will attend.
We will respect the result, regardless of whether people are for or against it.
The emergency department accepts patients day or night.
We are grateful regardless of the amount.
fields.explain:
Ideal for the language of regulations / general application; highly universal.
The second clause is usually an impersonal clause:実施する・受け付ける・可能だ…
In ordinary conversation, with nouns it can be replaced by 〜を問わず.

• “Regardless of / not depending on …” → the second clause does not change according to the preceding condition.
• Used in rules/policies/announcements; formal/all-encompassing nuance.
• Goes well with familiar categories (年齢/性別/経験/国籍/天候/有無…).
fields.notes:
• Colloquial shortened form with a pair of opposites: 行く行かないにかかわらず (still correct but formal).
• Adding は for contrast: Nにかかわらずは (rarely used) → it is better to avoid 〜かどうかにかかわらずは.
• In designing forms/signs: “〜の如何を問わず” is a very formal equivalent expression. | Variant: ～にかかわりなく
mistakes: Confusing it with “にもかかわらず” (although): the function is completely different.
Dropping かどうか after a verb/adjective: × 行くにかかわらず → ○ 行くかどうかにかかわらず.
Using it with a clause of strong personal volition does not suit the style (except in official announcements).

rows: Used with N or かどうか
<ruby>国籍<rt>こくせき</rt></ruby>にかかわらず
<ruby>年齢<rt>ねんれい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>関<rt>かか</rt></ruby>わりなく

fields.meaning: When it comes to…, in the field of…
examples: When it comes to running fast, I'm confident I won't lose to anyone.
Company B's brand has a good reputation when it comes to design.
When it comes to knowledge of history, no one in the class can match Sato.
When it comes to analytical skills, she is head and shoulders above the rest.
When it comes to endurance, this athlete is among the best in the world.
Our company does not compromise when it comes to quality control.
fields.explain:
It is a sentence of praise; used when introducing abilities, in PR, sports commentary, and personnel evaluations.
The noun must be a measurable area of skill/quality.
Combines with set phrases of praise: 〜は一番だ／随一だ／ピカイチだ／右に出るものはいない.

• Highlights a strength in a specific area; used to compare relative/absolute superiority.
• The second clause usually goes with expressions of not being inferior / being the best / being impressive.
• Not suitable for direct complaints; for criticism, use 苦手だ/下手だ.
fields.notes:
• Can be used for groups: 日本チームにかけては守備が堅い.
• Implies a relative comparison with the rest of the set (社内/リーグ/地域など).
• The order of elements can be reversed for emphasis: 守備にかけてはこのチームが最強だ.
explain: After ［～にかけては］comes a sentence expressing a positive evaluation.
examples: 1. 足の速さにかけては、彼は町で一番だ。
When it comes to running fast, he is the best in town.
2. 歌のうまさにかけては、彼に勝てる人はいない。
When it comes to singing well, no one can beat him.
mistakes: Using it with a noun that is not a “field”: × 天気にかけては → use については instead.
Using it for direct criticism: × 彼は時間管理にかけては下手だ → unnatural; use 彼は時間管理が下手だ.
Confusing it with 〜にかけて (until/spanning); exam questions often set traps with the two meanings.

fields.meaning:
（もちろん）～のほうがいい
Naturally… would be better
examples: "Can I do that job even without experience?"
"Yes, it's better if you have experience, but it's fine if you don't."
Cheap rent is of course best, but that said, being far from the station is a problem.
If you can become a full-time employee rather than a part-timer, nothing could be better.
When shopping online, you can never be too careful.
Of course it's best if nothing happens, but just in case, I always take out insurance when I travel abroad.
fields.explain:
Used in recommendations and principles of life/experience:保険は入っておくに越したことはない。
It is not a command; it implies “if possible, …”.
In conversation it can be shortened:早いに越したことないよ。
With Aな/N, the standard form is である + に越したことはない (formal).
fields.notes:
examples: 1. 早めに出発するに越したことはない。
Nothing beats leaving early.
2. 安全であるに越したことはないが、過剰な警戒は不要だ。
Being safe is best, but excessive caution is unnecessary.
3. 初めてなら、説明書を読んでから始めるに越したことはない。
If it's your first time, it's best to read the manual before starting.
4. 無理をしないに越したことはない。
It's better not to overdo it.
5. 経験があるに越したことはないが、必須ではない。
Having experience is better, but it's not required.
mistakes: Forgetting “である” with Aな/N in written language: ×安全に越したことはない（acceptable in conversation; in written language use: 安全であるに～）。
Taking it as a firm command → wrong nuance; this is gentle advice.
Overusing it for something already decided → sounds redundant: ×会場はここに決めた。広いに越したことはない。
JLPT N2–N1: Recognize it when it appears with できれば／やはり; it carries the sense of “something everyone agrees on”.

Specific advice; less of an “obvious” sense

examples: For a Sunday night, the train is crowded.
For someone who has always played sports, he often catches colds and stays home.
My father looks young for 50.

fields.explain:
Expresses an impression of something "unusual" based on the common standard of the group/condition that N indicates.
The second clause is a judgment/evaluation. Rarely used for commands/wishes.
Goes well with words for quantity/price/age to emphasize "compared with the norm":値段 にしては …,年齢 にしては …
More objective nuance than わりに(は) with a personal N; clearly emphasizes the "group standard".

• Used to state an evaluation contrary to expectations based on a standard N/V: "even though/compared with being…, …".
• The standard N is a general group/identity/condition (children, beginners, spring…).
• The second clause is usually a remark or subjective evaluation that is surprising compared with the standard.
• Different from のに: it does not express a disappointed cause-and-effect relationship, but a comparison with the "expected standard".
fields.notes:
• Best used with objective standards (age, occupation, experience, season…); avoid vague standards that are hard to define.
• The second clause is usually an adjective/verb expressing evaluation: いい／悪い／多い／少ない／うまい／下手 など.
• With concrete figures: 1000円にしては…, 3ヶ月にしては… make the sentence objective and convincing.
mistakes: Using it with commands/wishes: 子どもにしては早く寝なさい（unnatural). Use it for evaluations.
Confusing it with わりに(は): when the standard is an objective group (初心者, 子ども), prefer にしては.
Using it for obvious facts with no element of surprise → loses the "unusual" meaning.
Making N too vague: 彼にしては… but without information about the "standard" it will be hard to understand in the exam.

rows: Even though/compared with the expected standard
The standard is a general group/identity; clear surprise.
<ruby>初心者<rt>しょしんしゃ</rt></ruby>にしてはうまい。
The standard is subjective/personal; milder surprise.
<ruby>年齢<rt>ねんれい</rt></ruby>のわりに<ruby>若<rt>わか</rt></ruby>く<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>える。
Hypothetical concession, broad scope, not necessarily a group standard.
<ruby>安<rt>やす</rt></ruby>いにしても<ruby>品質<rt>ひんしつ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>大事<rt>だいじ</rt></ruby>だ。
Opposite meaning: the result matches expectations, usually praise.
<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>いだけあって<ruby>品質<rt>ひんしつ</rt></ruby>がいい。
Emphasizes the contradiction between reality and the speaker's expectations; strong emotion.

examples: Even if you're not interested, I'd like you to reply whether you're going or not.
I don't think even the company president is blaming him.
Even if you apologize, you should apologize a bit more properly.
Even if you're busy, it's not good not to let us know that you will be absent.
No matter how busy you are, sleep is important.
Even if you go, get ready before you go.
fields.explain:
Combines well with emphatic words たとえ/いくら/どんなに.
The second clause is usually the speaker's evaluation/position.
V-たにしても is used when acknowledging something that has already happened; V-るにしても for a future supposition.
Compared with としても: slightly more formal/stiff; compared with にしろ/にせよ: softer.

• Concession: Even if X, Y (position unchanged).
• Acknowledging a fact: Even though X has happened, the conclusion is still Y.
• Evaluation by a standard: Even for/at the level of N, … (beyond/different from expectations).
• Listing: N1にしてもN2にしても: whether it is A or B, the conclusion is the same.
fields.notes:
• “Nにしても…” can be translated flexibly: “even… ”, “even if…”.
• In literature/speeches, “であるにしても” increases objectivity.
• The pairing can be extended to more than two elements: AにしてもBにしてもCにしても…
mistakes: Confusing it with ～にしては (deviation from expectations) and ～としても (neutral supposition).
Dropping “だ/である” before にしても with N/Na in written language.
A direct command after にしても can sound harsh; consider the situation.
Use V-たにしても when the event has already happened; V-るにしても for a supposition.

rows: <ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>くとしても<ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>する。
Formal/stiff; often followed by a command
<ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しいにしろ<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>なさい。
Expresses deviation from expectations, not concession

fields.explain: ◎ A written-language expression meaning "because of ~". Often used in notices.
fields.notes:
explain: A stiff sentence style. Often used in formal situations or in business documents. ⏐ examples: 1. この機械はただ今調整中につき、ご使用になれません。
This machine is currently being adjusted, so it cannot be used.
2. 本日は祭日につき、休業させていただきます。
Today is a national holiday, so we will be closed.

examples: Whenever I see news like this, I think politicians can't be trusted.
He complains at every opportunity, which is a real problem.
Whenever I see children studying hard, I think it's really good that I'm doing this job.
That customer complains about every little thing, so it's really troublesome.
fields.explain: ◎ An expression indicating the cause that leads to some action or state of mind.
fields.notes: As a fixed idiomatic expression, used in the forms 「何事につけ」 and 「何かにつけ」, meaning “in any case” and “every time there is some occasion,” respectively.

examples: As I've gotten older, my eyesight has gotten worse.
With the spread of personal computers, more and more people feel they can no longer write kanji correctly.
fields.explain: ◎ When one thing or state changes, another thing changes along with it.

examples: Along with the decrease in the number of children, the number of schools is also decreasing.
Because I'm getting married, I will be moving.
fields.explain: ◎ An expression describing a change that arises as a result of some other change.
fields.notes: An even more formal way of saying 「にともなって」.

examples: Along with the economic recovery, consumption is increasing.
As the population grew, traffic congestion became more serious.
With the construction of the dam, the surrounding environment changed greatly.
We would like to inform you of the procedures for changing your address in connection with personnel transfers.
With the economic downturn, we reviewed our hiring plans.
With the completion of the station
fields.explain:
Emphasizes relationships that are systemic/policy-related/social phenomena; suits a serious style.
The second clause is a result, effect, or countermeasure; avoid direct commands except in notices.
Often appears with academic vocabulary:変化,影響,増加,減少,実施,見直し,…

- Meaning 1 (simultaneous change): “Along with/at the same time as A, B also changes/continues.”
- Meaning 2 (accompaniment/consequence): “A brings about B (consequence/effect/measure).”
- More formal than ～につれて; can be used in formal spoken language, written language, and administrative notices.
fields.notes:
• “伴う” is a formal Sino-Japanese word; in headings/notices “に伴い/に伴う” is commonly used.
• If you want to emphasize a clear cause–result relationship, consider ため/ので; “にともなって” is neutral and describes an accompanying relationship.
• Often used in a nominalized passive form: N + に伴う + N (effects/measures/costs…).
mistakes: Using it for a single, instantaneous event → does not fit the “process/accompaniment” nuance.
Confusing the modifier function: “に伴う + N” must come before a noun.
JLPT trap when choosing between につれて and にともなって where the second clause is a “measure/effect” → prefer にともなって.

rows: Formal; used for changes and accompanying consequences
<ruby>増加<rt>ぞうか</rt></ruby>にともなって<ruby>対策<rt>たいさく</rt></ruby>が<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>。

fields.meaning: Is precisely…, is nothing other than…
examples: We were able to achieve our goal for no other reason than the cooperation of those around us.
The coach being strict with him is nothing other than a sign of high expectations.
Her passing is nothing other than the result of hard work.
Parents scold their children precisely because they love them.
The success of the new business is nothing other than the fruit of the efforts of all the employees.
More and more people now think that brain death is nothing other than human death.
fields.explain:
Used to emphasize the essence/truth/origin of something.
Strong, formal nuance; suitable for reports, essays, and speeches.
Often used with vocabulary of causal relationships:原因,結果,目的,事実,誤解,…

- Strong affirmation “is precisely …/is nothing other than …”, used to draw a conclusion about the essence/core cause.
- Often appears in official statements, argumentative writing, and press releases; a nuance of certainty and decisiveness.
fields.notes:
• The form “A は B にほかならない” is suitable for concluding a paragraph: redefining A as B.
• “…からにほかならない” emphasizes the sole reason; suitable for refuting rumors/speculation.
• Not used when the speaker is only making a vague conjecture; requires a firm stance or grounds. meaning_vi: is precisely, is nothing other than ～ ⏐ explain: Used when you want to make the assertion “there is nothing other than that”, “it is exactly that”
A stiff sentence style. ⏐ examples: 1. 合格したのは、彼の努力の結果にほかならない。
Passing the exam is nothing other than the result of his efforts.
2. 彼があなたをからかうのは、まさに愛情表現にほかならない。
His teasing you is nothing other than an expression of affection.
mistakes: Using it directly with an adjective (×嬉しいにほかならない) → convert it to a nominalization: 嬉しさにほかならない.
Using it when not yet certain/still conjecturing → contradicts the strong affirmative nuance.
Confusing it with ～にすぎない (opposite meaning): one elevates with strong affirmation, the other downplays the degree.

rows: <ruby>成功<rt>せいこう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>努力<rt>どりょく</rt></ruby>にほかならない。

examples: Although I've been studying English for many years, I still can't speak it well.
Despite being injured, he played in the match again today.
Although he had a high fever, he went to work.
Despite the late hour, a large number of people rushed to the hospital.
I hear that this game console sells well despite being expensive.
Although I was being careful, I failed again.
fields.explain:
Formal/objective nuance: suitable for writing, presentations, and announcements.
Emphasizes a “paradoxical” result rather than the speaker's emotions (unlike ～のに, which often carries a nuance of annoyance/regret).
The first clause is a “fact/obvious condition” or a “general expectation”; information that is still conjecture should not be used.
The sentence can be split with “。それにもかかわらず、～。” for more emphasis.

Expresses “although/despite A, B (a result contrary to common sense/unexpected)”. Character: formal, more objective than ～のに. Emphasizes a strong contrast between the reality A and the result B.
• Implies “contrary to common sense, expectations, or obvious conditions”.
• Often appears in written language, news, reports, and speeches.
• Not (or very rarely) used to state wishes/give direct commands; suitable for describing facts and evaluations.
fields.notes:
• With Aな/N, “である” makes the sentence natural and consistent with written style.
• Can be combined with statistical data or news headlines to increase formality.
• If you want to express personal emotions, consider using ～のに instead of ～にもかかわらず. explain: Used when you want to say that the result turned out different from what was expected from the reality of ～ ⏐ examples: 1. 雨にもかかわらず、大勢の人々が集まった。
A large number of people gathered despite the rain.
2. 見たにもかかわらず、彼は見なかったと言った。
Even though he saw it, he said he hadn't.
mistakes: Using it with direct commands/suggestions makes the sentence awkward: avoid “にもかかわらず、来てください” in formal writing.
Dropping “である” after N/Aな in written language makes it less natural: “学生にもかかわらず” → should be “学生であるにもかかわらず”.
Confusing it with “のに”: exam questions often ask you to choose the pattern with the right nuance; official documents prefer “にもかかわらず”.

rows: Casual, strong emotion, common in speech
Objective, written language, emphasizes “contrary to expectation”
